findings.title: GhostShares 2: Grok Apps Exposed xAI's Business Secrets and People's Private Data (Claroc Research)
findings.summary_md: Claroc Research, authored by Asaf Aprozper, published the primary research on November 10, 2026. The team resolved 43,601 names under grok.me by subdomain discovery, opened the first page of 43,551 addresses from the public internet while signed in to nothing, found 37,571 still online and 35,578 of those (94.7 percent) opening for anyone, and only 1,993 answered HTTP 401. The post documents the Grok Build publish panel offering 'Anyone with the link' preselected, a team app whose generated sign-in logic let an uninvited Google account read, edit and delete records, and an estimate of roughly 650 to 800 apps holding private data, and it dates the start of the work to November 8, 2026, the SpaceXSI security.txt notification to that same afternoon, the report of the remaining 22 staff apps to November 9, and the vendor reply to November 10.

findings.title: GhostShares: A Shared Muse Chat Exposed Prep for a Confidential Call With a Frontier AI Lab Leader (Claroc Research, GhostShares 1)
findings.summary_md: Three weeks before the Grok Build findings, the same team published the first GhostShares report on Meta's Muse assistant, which publishes shared conversations as pages that open for anyone holding the link. The post explains the technique the Grok research later reused: Muse named each share's address after the conversation title, passive DNS and subdomain discovery listed those hostnames, and an incognito session with no login returned personal files and internal company documents. On October 20, 2026, after Ars Technica asked about the findings, Meta told the outlet it was suspending the feature; Claroc rechecked 40 shares that day and none opened, though the hostnames and titles remained in passive DNS history.

findings.title: Railway security incident: finding the apps your employees deployed (Claroc Research)
findings.summary_md: Published October 22, 2026 and updated October 26, this Claroc post covers the platform-side version of the same problem: environment variables holding AI provider keys, payment keys, database passwords and cloud credentials sitting in a hosted build platform. The post records the revocation request Railway's status page linked at 21:48 UTC on October 21, 2026, and shows the method Claroc later reused for AI-built apps, which is enumerating what a company's employees deployed outside IT's view. It is relevant background rather than part of the Grok Build disclosure, since the Grok research does not cite it.

findings.title: LinkDrift: How Leaked Links Exposed Internal Files at Fortune 500 Companies (Claroc Research)
findings.summary_md: Claroc's October 5, 2026 LinkDrift report established the access-control pattern the Grok Build research extends: share links already circulating in malware logs and public indexes still opened corporate material with no exploit and no login. The dataset covered 326 organizations, with about 800 accessible links among Fortune 500 companies and sensitive or internal material confirmed at 19 of them; one link exposed a folder reporting 8,496 files and 749.1 GB. The Grok Build post does not cite LinkDrift, but both rest on the finding that an unguessable URL handed out as an access control keeps working for anyone who obtains it.

findings.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI (Ars Technica)
findings.summary_md: Dan Goodin reported on November 10, 2026 that Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, was leaking proprietary business information and sensitive secrets from thousands of users through share links. Research from security firm Claroc showed the exposed data included internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers, including two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI itself. A design decision by the platform's developers made it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects despite randomized URLs.

findings.title: Grok Build vibe-coding agent allowed sensitive data to leak from thousands of users including SpaceXSI (Engadget)
findings.summary_md: Engadget reported on November 11, 2026 that the way Grok handles links to apps allowed them to be exposed publicly by certain types of DNS services, according to Claroc. Sensitive information involving employees was leaked from a hospital group, a fire department, and SpaceXSI itself, including an onboarding plan, a sales territory map of 594 strategic accounts, eight X advertising proposals, and four live advertiser account boards. The researchers called these pages GhostShares because they can be found and opened by people who were never given the link.

findings.title: Over 35,000 Grok-Built Apps Exposed Online, Some Leaking Confidential Data and Passwords (The Hacker News)
findings.summary_md: The Hacker News reported on November 11, 2026 that of the 37,571 Grok-built apps Claroc found online, 35,578 were open to anyone without a sign-in, including 24 apps built by staff at X and SpaceXSI. Most of the open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators, but about one in ten contained internal business or personal data, such as a confidential onboarding plan, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential. SpaceXSI removed all 24 staff apps after Claroc's report but not other users' apps, and open apps contained internal data from 30 other organizations.
